name: Inspect sites and run the safety committee
summary: Each week a site safety coordinator, or on smaller projects a coordinator who covers several sites, walks every active project with a checklist, records unsafe conditions such as missing guardrails, open floor holes and poor housekeeping, and stops work that puts someone in immediate danger. Once a month the walk is the joint health and safety committee inspection, with a worker member alongside. The superintendent assigns each finding to the responsible trade with a due date, and the coordinator follows up until it is closed; trades that repeat findings get written notices, back-charges or workers removed. The slow part is getting subcontractors to correct findings, which can take days to weeks, and closing items in the system when coordinators move between sites.

baseline.org_archetype: A national Canadian general contractor acting as constructor on about 220 active projects, with 45 site safety coordinators and 6 regional safety managers.
baseline.notes: One case is one weekly safety inspection of one project, including follow-up of its findings; quarterly committee meetings are attached to the inspection that falls before them.

trigger: The weekly inspection for a project falls due on the coordinator's schedule.
end_state: Every finding from the inspection has been corrected and closed in the safety system, and the inspection score is included in the regional safety report.

volume.seasonality: Follows the number of active sites; slightly higher in summer when more short projects run.

evidence.note: About 220 active projects (organisation file driver) times 4.33 weeks a month gives about 950 inspections.

surge.cause: Ministry of Labour construction inspection blitz or a serious incident on another company site, prompting extra company-wide inspections

evidence.note: Ontario runs focused construction inspection campaigns (for example on falls) most years; the company response size is an estimate.
Touch time per inspection of about 3.3 hours including travel, times about 950 inspections at 130 productive hours.
Assigning findings, verifying corrections and chairing quarterly committee meetings.
Worker member of the joint health and safety committee or health and safety representative, on the monthly inspection only.
Reviews repeat infractions and the weekly inspection scores for the region.

systems.name: Safety management system (hazard assessments, inspections, incidents, training records)
Project management platform (drawings, RFIs, submittals, daily logs, change events)
Reporting and dashboards (Excel cost reports, Power BI)

resources.name: Pickup trucks for superintendents, foremen and safety staff

steps.name: Prepare for the inspection
steps.description: The safety coordinator opens the project's record in the safety system, reads open findings from last week, recent hazard and near miss reports and the three-week look-ahead schedule, and picks the high-risk activities to look at closely.

next.condition: coordinator covers several sites and drives there
coordinator is based on this site

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

steps.name: Drive to the site
steps.description: The coordinator drives a company pickup from the office or another project to this site, often combining two or three sites in a day.

evidence.note: Share of sites without a resident coordinator and drive times are estimates; 45 coordinators for about 220 projects means most cover several sites.

steps.name: Sign in and agree the walk with the superintendent
steps.description: The coordinator signs in, waits for site access where the building is occupied (hospital wards, schools in session) and meets the superintendent to hear what work is under way and which trades are on site today.

evidence.note: About one weekly inspection in four is the monthly committee or representative inspection. Escort and infection-control sign-in waits at occupied hospitals are estimates.

steps.name: Release the worker member for the inspection
steps.description: The superintendent asks the foreman to release the worker member of the joint health and safety committee, or the health and safety representative on a smaller project, so that they can walk the site with the coordinator.

control.basis: Ontario OHSA s.9: a designated worker member inspects the workplace at least monthly

evidence.note: IHSA: JHSC or health and safety representative inspects the project monthly and the committee meets at least every three months. Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Worker member inspects alongside
steps.description: The worker member walks with the coordinator, talks to workers from each trade about their concerns, adds findings from the workers' side and signs the monthly inspection record.

control.basis: Ontario OHSA s.9: monthly workplace inspection by a committee worker member

evidence.note: IHSA: JHSC or health and safety representative inspects the project monthly and the committee meets at least every three months. Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Walk the site with the checklist
steps.description: The coordinator walks every active floor and the perimeter with the inspection checklist, checking guardrails and floor-hole covers, scaffolds and ladders, excavations, temporary electrical, crane and rigging, housekeeping, fire protection and PPE, and photographs each finding.

error.defect_description: A hazard in an area not visited or behind a closed door is missed.

control.basis: COR workplace inspection element and the site safety plan: documented weekly inspection

next.condition: a hazard puts someone in immediate danger

evidence.note: COR audits check documented inspections; duration and the imminent-danger share are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Stop the unsafe work
steps.description: The coordinator stops the work at once, for example a worker at an unprotected edge or an unshored trench, tells the trade's foreman what must change before work restarts and informs the superintendent.

control.basis: Constructor's duty under Ontario OHSA s.23 and the company stop-work authority

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

steps.name: Trade corrects the imminent hazard
steps.description: The subcontractor's foreman has the crew install guardrails, tie off, shore the excavation or remove the worker before restarting; the coordinator checks it before leaving the area.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

steps.name: Record findings in the safety system
steps.description: Back in the site trailer the coordinator enters each finding in the safety system with its photo, location, hazard category, responsible trade and a risk rating, and scores the inspection.

error.defect_description: Finding assigned to the wrong trade or described too vaguely to act on.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

steps.name: Assign corrective actions with the superintendent
steps.description: The coordinator goes through the findings with the superintendent, who confirms which trade owns each, sets a due date by risk, and decides which items his own crews will fix.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

steps.name: Issue the inspection report
steps.description: The coordinator issues the report from the safety system by email to the superintendent, project manager and each subcontractor with findings, and posts it on the site safety board.

control.basis: Ontario OHSA s.9: committee inspection findings reported to the committee; COR documentation

evidence.note: Share of inspections with at least one open finding is an estimate.

steps.name: Trades correct the findings
steps.description: Each subcontractor with findings assigns them to its foreman, fixes them in the course of work and tells the superintendent when done; many need materials, a lift or a crew to come back to the floor.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

steps.name: Verify corrections on the site walk
steps.description: The superintendent or assistant superintendent checks each corrected item during the daily site walk and marks it corrected on the printed list or in the app.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

steps.name: Close actions in the safety system
steps.description: On the next visit the coordinator checks the superintendent's list against the site and closes each corrected action in the safety system, re-opening any item that is not fixed.

next.condition: a finding is not corrected or repeats

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

steps.name: Issue a safety infraction notice
steps.description: The coordinator writes a safety infraction notice to the subcontractor naming the uncorrected or repeated finding, the rule broken and the deadline, and copies the project manager for the subcontractor performance file.

control.basis: Subcontract safety clauses and the company progressive enforcement procedure

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

steps.name: Decide on enforcement
steps.description: The regional safety manager reviews the trade's record and decides on a back-charge for the GC fixing the item, removal of a worker from site, or a meeting with the subcontractor's owner, and records the decision.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

steps.name: Check whether a committee meeting is due
steps.description: The coordinator checks the committee calendar; on projects with a joint health and safety committee, a meeting is due at least every three months and the inspection findings go on its agenda.

evidence.note: IHSA: JHSC or health and safety representative inspects the project monthly and the committee meets at least every three months. Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Hold the joint health and safety committee meeting
steps.description: The superintendent co-chairs the committee meeting with the worker co-chair, reviews inspection findings, incidents and worker concerns since the last meeting, and agrees written recommendations.

control.basis: Ontario OHSA s.9: joint health and safety committee meets at least every three months

evidence.note: IHSA: JHSC or health and safety representative inspects the project monthly and the committee meets at least every three months. Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Post minutes and track recommendations
steps.description: The coordinator types the minutes, posts them on the site safety board, files them in the safety system and logs each recommendation with an owner and due date.

control.basis: Ontario OHSA s.9: committee minutes and recommendations kept and available

evidence.note: IHSA: JHSC or health and safety representative inspects the project monthly and the committee meets at least every three months. Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Review inspection scores for the region
steps.description: The regional safety manager opens the weekly inspection dashboard, compares this site's score and open items with other sites, and raises poor trends with the operations manager.

next.condition: included in the weekly or monthly report

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

exceptions.name: Imminent danger stop-work
exceptions.description: A worker is exposed to an immediate hazard; work stops until the trade corrects it.

exceptions.name: Uncorrected or repeated finding
exceptions.description: A trade does not fix a finding by the due date; a written notice and possibly enforcement by the safety manager follow, and the loop repeats until corrected.

exceptions.name: Quarterly committee meeting
exceptions.description: The committee meets, reviews findings and issues recommendations.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from the inspection falling due to all findings closed and reported
benchmarks.population: Weekly site safety inspections on Canadian commercial building projects

evidence.note: Most findings are due within one to seven days; closing in the system waits for the next weekly visit. No published benchmark found.

benchmarks.unit: workplace inspections per month by the committee worker member
benchmarks.population: Ontario construction projects with a JHSC or health and safety representative

pain_points.description: Subcontractors take days to weeks to correct findings, and the same findings recur on the next walk.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

pain_points.description: Coordinators covering several sites lose an hour or more a day driving, and actions stay open in the system until their next visit.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

pain_points.description: Findings are photographed on site and re-typed in the trailer, so reports lag the walk.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

sources.title: JHSC / Health and Safety Representative
sources.supports: Ontario construction projects: health and safety representative for 6 to 19 workers, joint health and safety committee for 20 or more workers on projects over three months; monthly workplace inspection; committee meets at least every three months; certified members on projects of 50 or more workers; worker trades committee on large multi-trade projects.

sources.title: COR Process
sources.supports: COR needs an external audit score of at least 80%, is valid three years with annual internal maintenance audits of at least 60%, and audits review documentation, interviews and observations.

assumptions: The worker member of the committee is modelled with the carpenter role because most worker members come from the company's own carpentry and concrete crews; the organisation file does not list a worker role for this process.

Ontario committee rules are used as the reference because the head office and about half the field work are in Ontario; Alberta and the Atlantic provinces have similar committee or representative duties.
Correcting findings is done by subcontractors and costs them, not the company, so it carries no touch time here.
Loaded costs and shift patterns come from the organisation file.
